difficultyReason: Statistical inference layered over a causal claim: the argument compares two cohorts but leaves a selection-bias alternative open. The correct answer rules out that subtle third alternative. Trap (A) strengthens a neighboring claim about dosage; trap (D) introduces an unwarranted comparison.
stimulus: Patients treated for hypertension at the Ledford clinic were prescribed either drug P or drug Q, depending on which was in stock the day they first visited. Over five years, patients who received drug P had 22 percent fewer cardiac events than those who received drug Q. Since the two groups were otherwise similar in age, weight, and medical history, researchers concluded that drug P probably provides better cardiac protection than drug Q.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients who received higher doses of drug P experienced greater reductions in blood pressure than those who received lower doses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug P and drug Q are prescribed with roughly equal frequency at other hypertension clinics in the region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients who received drug P were no more likely than those who received drug Q to also be taking cholesterol-lowering medications during the study.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At a different clinic, patients treated with drug P had fewer cardiac events than patients treated with a third hypertension drug.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drug P is somewhat more expensive per dose than drug Q.

explanations.correct: The researchers controlled for age, weight, and medical history, but a concurrent cholesterol drug could be the real driver of drug P patients' better outcomes. (C) rules out that alternative, making the causal attribution to drug P substantially more plausible.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about dose-response for blood pressure, not about comparative cardiac protection.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — prescribing frequency elsewhere doesn't address whether drug P actually protects the heart.
explanations.D: Unwarranted comparison — a third drug's performance doesn't address the P-versus-Q contrast or rule out confounding at Ledford.
explanations.E: Tangential — cost has no bearing on clinical efficacy.

difficultyReason: Economic argument combining an analogy with a causal claim. The correct answer closes the analogical gap by ruling out a feature unique to the reference case. Trap (B) strengthens a sister conclusion about revenue; trap (E) is an alternative cause dressed as support.
stimulus: Economist: Three decades ago, the province of Harwell gradually phased out its personal income tax while raising its sales tax. Within ten years, Harwell's per capita economic output had grown substantially faster than that of neighboring provinces. The province of Brenmark is now considering a similar tax shift. Critics argue that the shift worked in Harwell only because Harwell's tourist economy absorbed the new sales tax. Still, the same tax shift would probably accelerate growth in Brenmark as well.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Brenmark has a slightly larger population than Harwell had at the time of its tax shift.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tax revenues in Harwell rose, rather than fell, during the decade following the shift.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Brenmark already attracts a proportion of its revenue from tourists that is comparable to what Harwell's tourist share was before the shift.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of Harwell's accelerated growth during that decade occurred in sectors unrelated to tourism, such as manufacturing and software.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Around the time Harwell phased out its income tax, a neighboring province subsidized a new rail line into Harwell's largest city.

explanations.correct: The critics' objection is that tourism, not the tax shift, drove Harwell's growth. (D) undermines that alternative by showing the growth came from non-tourist sectors, closing the analogical gap between Harwell and Brenmark.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — a modest population difference doesn't address the tourism objection.
explanations.B: Strengthens a different conclusion — about revenue, not growth.
explanations.C: Addresses tourist share but cuts both ways: it could just as easily support the critics' view that the shift depends on a tourism buffer.
explanations.E: Weakens — supplies a rival explanation (the rail subsidy) for Harwell's growth.

difficultyReason: EXCEPT format over an ethical argument: four choices strengthen, one fails to. Test-takers under time pressure tend to pick the first strengthener rather than scanning for the odd-one-out. The non-strengthener (C) is irrelevant rather than weakening, which makes it harder to spot.
stimulus: Ethicist: Public universities should require every undergraduate to complete a course in formal logic. Studies of college graduates consistently show that those who took such a course later reported fewer regrets about major life decisions than graduates who did not. A course in formal logic therefore probably improves students' ability to make decisions they will not later regret.
questionStem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the ethicist's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students who enter college with a preference for formal logic do not consistently report fewer regrets about life decisions than students without that preference.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exercises used in formal logic courses directly train students to identify unstated assumptions in everyday reasoning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A course in formal logic typically satisfies one of several general-education requirements at most public universities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Graduates who took a formal logic course report making the same kinds of major life decisions as graduates who did not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Self-reported regret correlates closely with independent measures of decision quality in long-term outcome studies.

explanations.correct: (C) is accurate but irrelevant: how the course fits into graduation requirements has no bearing on whether formal logic improves decision-making. It neither rules out an alternative nor confirms any load-bearing link, so it fails to strengthen.
explanations.A: Strengthens — rules out the selection-bias alternative that logic-minded students simply regret less.
explanations.B: Strengthens — supplies the unstated mechanism connecting logic training to better decisions.
explanations.D: Strengthens — rules out the alternative that the two groups face different kinds of decisions.
explanations.E: Strengthens — validates the self-report measure that the study relies on.

difficultyReason: Statistical inference in an environmental argument where the correct answer addresses a subtle selection threat (which sites were sampled). Trap (A) strengthens a sister claim; trap (E) introduces an alternative cause.
stimulus: Ecologist: Since protected status was extended to the Morrin estuary twelve years ago, the number of adult saltmarsh sparrows counted during our annual surveys has risen by 40 percent. Sparrow populations in comparable unprotected estuaries have declined over the same period. The protected designation has therefore probably caused the sparrow population to recover at Morrin.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At Morrin, the reproductive success rate of saltmarsh sparrows was already higher than the regional average before protection was granted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The annual surveys at Morrin have been conducted using the same survey routes and methods throughout the twelve-year period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some unprotected estuaries in the region have seen increases in the populations of other shorebird species during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protected status at Morrin restricts public access but does not restrict the use of nearby agricultural land.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The annual surveys at Morrin were expanded to cover additional marsh areas five years after protected status was granted.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that the rising count reflects changes in survey methodology rather than a real population increase. (B) rules this out by confirming methodological consistency, so the 40-percent rise is more plausibly a real recovery caused by protection.
explanations.A: Weakens — a pre-existing reproductive advantage suggests the recovery might have happened without protection.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — other species' trends don't bear on saltmarsh sparrows at Morrin.
explanations.D: Tangential — the access restriction's scope doesn't address whether the population actually rose because of protection.
explanations.E: Weakens — expanding the survey area inflates counts for reasons unrelated to population recovery.

difficultyReason: Nested reasoning: a predictive claim rests on an analogy plus an implicit mechanism about consumer behavior. The correct answer confirms the mechanism rather than bolstering the analogy. Trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion about retention; trap (E) is a disguised weakener.
stimulus: Technology columnist: The new Velora smart speaker displays on-screen captions for every spoken response. When an earlier model without captions was tested, users who were hard of hearing abandoned it within two weeks at three times the rate of other users. Since captions directly address that group's difficulties, the Velora will probably retain hard-of-hearing users at roughly the same rate as other users.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the columnist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Users of the earlier model who remained after two weeks tended to continue using it for at least a year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among users of the earlier model who abandoned it, those who were hard of hearing cited difficulty understanding spoken responses more often than any other reason.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Velora's captions can be disabled through a setting in the companion app.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Velora costs somewhat more than the earlier model but is sold through the same retail channels.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several competing smart speakers released this year also include on-screen captions for spoken responses.

explanations.correct: The columnist assumes the earlier model's high abandonment rate among hard-of-hearing users was caused by difficulty understanding speech — the exact problem captions fix. (B) confirms that mechanism, making it far more plausible that adding captions will close the retention gap.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about long-term retention of users who already stayed, not about the hard-of-hearing abandonment gap.
explanations.C: Weakens — if users can disable captions, the mechanism may not operate for them.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — price and distribution don't speak to whether captions solve the retention problem.
explanations.E: Irrelevant — competitor features don't bear on whether the Velora will retain hard-of-hearing users.

difficultyReason: Historical-linguistic argument with a compared-scenarios structure. The correct answer rules out a non-obvious third alternative (prior exposure through trade). Trap (D) strengthens a neighboring claim about a different language family; trap (B) is opposite-direction.
stimulus: Linguist: Speakers of the now-extinct Kellish language used a suffix that marked the speaker's degree of certainty about a reported event. The same suffix, with nearly the same range of meanings, appears in texts written in Antoric, a language spoken a thousand kilometers away. Since the two languages had no known common ancestor, the simplest explanation is that Antoric borrowed the suffix from Kellish during a period of contact between the two communities.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antoric texts that use the suffix were composed at least two centuries after the earliest surviving Kellish texts that use it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several other Kellish grammatical features appear in the earliest Antoric texts that use the suffix.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most languages spoken in the broader region used some system for marking speaker certainty about reported events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Languages descended from a common ancestor of Antoric, spoken far to the north, also use suffixes to mark speaker certainty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trade goods of Kellish origin have been found in Antoric archaeological sites but not the other way around.

explanations.correct: If Antoric independently happened to develop a similar certainty suffix, that would undercut the borrowing claim. (B) rules that alternative out: the clustering of multiple Kellish features in the earliest Antoric texts that use the suffix is far more consistent with borrowing than with coincidence.
explanations.A: Weakly supportive but does not rule out independent development — chronology alone doesn't distinguish borrowing from coincidence.
explanations.C: Weakens — regional ubiquity makes independent development of such a suffix in Antoric more plausible.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about the Antoric family's inherited tendencies, which would actually undermine the borrowing explanation.
explanations.E: Consistent with contact but doesn't establish the linguistic borrowing specifically; it's at best weak background support.

difficultyReason: Historical causal argument with compared scenarios. The correct answer addresses a subtle reverse-causation threat. Trap (A) strengthens a sister claim about a different period; trap (D) introduces an unwarranted comparison.
stimulus: Historian: In the two decades after the introduction of mechanical printing in Delsar, the number of pamphlets published per capita rose fivefold, and the number of literate adults in the city's trade guilds roughly doubled. In neighboring Trelford, which did not adopt mechanical printing until much later, literacy rates in comparable guilds remained flat. Mechanical printing therefore probably caused the rise in guild literacy in Delsar.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the two decades before printing was introduced in Delsar, literacy rates in Delsar's trade guilds had been essentially constant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several Trelford printers traveled to Delsar to learn the new technology before returning home to set up their own presses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pamphlets published in Delsar during the period in question dealt largely with matters of commercial practice relevant to guild members.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cities elsewhere in the region that adopted mechanical printing at roughly the same time as Delsar did not experience comparable literacy gains.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many Delsar guild members began sending their children to informal schools during the period in question.

explanations.correct: A natural reverse-causation worry is that guilds were already becoming more literate — and that rising demand, not the press, caused the surge in pamphlets. (A) rules out that alternative by showing pre-printing literacy was flat, so the post-printing rise is more plausibly caused by the press.
explanations.B: Tangential — printer mobility doesn't speak to whether printing caused the literacy rise in Delsar.
explanations.C: Tempting, but content relevance alone doesn't rule out that literate guild members demanded the pamphlets rather than the press causing the literacy.
explanations.D: Weakens — if comparable cities with printing did not see the gains, the press is unlikely to be sufficient, undermining the causal attribution.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause (informal schooling) that would weaken rather than strengthen the press attribution.

difficultyReason: Policy argument with a nested causal chain (program feature → behavioral change → outcome). Correct answer confirms the middle link. Trap (B) is accurate but irrelevant; trap (C) strengthens a misreading of the argument.
stimulus: City planner: When Harford adopted evening parking meters on its main commercial street, foot traffic at nearby restaurants during dinner hours rose by 18 percent within six months. The meters discourage long-term parking by commuters, freeing spaces for diners. The meters are therefore probably responsible for the increase in dinner-hour foot traffic.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the city planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The revenue from the evening meters has been earmarked for maintenance of the commercial street's sidewalks and lighting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hourly meter rate during evening hours is the same as the rate during business hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restaurants near the commercial street that offer private parking lots reported similar increases in dinner-hour foot traffic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: After the meters were installed, the average length of time parked cars remained on the commercial street during dinner hours fell sharply.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several new restaurants opened on the commercial street during the six months following the meters' installation.

explanations.correct: The planner's causal chain has two links: meters shorten parking durations, and shorter durations free spaces for diners. (D) directly confirms the first link with observed data, making the full chain substantially more plausible.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — how the revenue is spent has no bearing on the mechanism.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — uniform pricing doesn't speak to whether the meters changed parking behavior.
explanations.C: Weakens — if restaurants with private lots saw similar gains, the meters are unlikely to be the cause.
explanations.E: Weakens — new restaurants supply an alternative cause for the traffic increase.

difficultyReason: Arts/statistical argument where the correct answer rules out a subtle self-selection threat. Trap (E) is a plausible strengthener for a misreading about all students; trap (A) strengthens a sister conclusion about adult learners.
stimulus: Music instructor: Among children at the Arris conservatory, those who begin piano lessons before age seven tend, on average, to achieve higher scores on sight-reading exams at age twelve than children who begin later. The earlier start therefore probably causes the stronger sight-reading performance.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the instructor's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adult students who begin piano lessons after age thirty tend to achieve lower sight-reading scores than those who began earlier in adulthood.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sight-reading exam at Arris is administered using the same format and difficulty level to all twelve-year-old students.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Among Arris children, age of starting piano lessons is not correlated with parental income or with prior exposure to other musical instruments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Teachers at Arris observe that early-starting students generally seem more confident during lessons than later-starting students.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students at Arris who practice more hours per week tend to score higher on sight-reading exams than students who practice less.

explanations.correct: The natural alternative is that early-starting students are systematically different — wealthier families, more musical households — and that those factors, not the early start, drive sight-reading scores. (C) rules out both confounders, making the causal attribution to age-of-start more plausible.
explanations.A: Strengthens a sister conclusion about adult learners and doesn't bear on the causal claim about children.
explanations.B: Rules out a measurement concern but does nothing to address the underlying self-selection threat.
explanations.D: Accurate but tangential — confidence during lessons doesn't establish that the early start caused the exam-score gap.
explanations.E: Plausible strengthener for a misreading that practice hours explain the effect; it actually introduces an alternative cause.

difficultyReason: Medical argument with a nested causal claim relying on timing. The correct answer rules out a reverse-causation alternative. Trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion; trap (D) is accurate but irrelevant.
stimulus: Researcher: A large study of adults over age sixty has found that those who walk briskly for at least thirty minutes a day are significantly less likely to show early markers of cognitive decline than those who are less active. Brisk walking probably helps prevent early cognitive decline in older adults.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Older adults who engage in strenuous cardiovascular exercise other than walking also show fewer early markers of cognitive decline than less active peers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Study participants who began walking briskly only after enrolling in the study showed fewer cognitive-decline markers five years later than those who remained inactive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Among study participants, the difference in cognitive-decline markers between brisk walkers and less active adults grew larger with each year of follow-up.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Brisk walking has been shown to improve cardiovascular health in adults of all ages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Study participants who reported the most enjoyment of their daily activities were slightly more likely to walk briskly than those who reported less enjoyment.

explanations.correct: The central threat is reverse causation: people whose cognition is already declining may simply walk less. (B) addresses this by showing that adults who took up brisk walking after enrolling — and so could not have selected into walking on the basis of prior cognitive health — still showed fewer decline markers, strongly supporting the causal direction the researcher claims.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — that cardiovascular exercise broadly helps cognition — rather than the specific brisk-walking claim, and doesn't rule out reverse causation.
explanations.C: Consistent with the conclusion but equally consistent with cognitive decline making people progressively less active; does not rule out reverse causation.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant to cognitive decline specifically.
explanations.E: Weakens — introduces mood or life satisfaction as an alternative cause of both walking and better cognition.
